I've been working these fields for 50 years, since I was a teenager. I only finished middle school, but I know this land better than any book. My farm is 10.1 mu, which is neither small nor big—just right for me and my wife. My son works in a factory in the city and sends money home, which helps when I need to buy fertilizer and diesel for the well pump, but I still count every yuan.

I split the land like this: 6 mu goes to wheat in the winter, then maize in the summer on the same patch. That is the double-crop system everyone around Quzhou does. Another 2 mu is cotton, and the last 2.1 mu is stevia. I started stevia two years ago because the dealer in town said the factory buys the dried leaves, and my neighbor Lao Zhang did okay with it, so I copied him.

For the wheat, I am planting the same improved Jimai variety as Old Wang across the road. He got nearly 500 jin per mu last year. I put one 50-kilogram bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base fertilizer when I sow in October—I am not cutting that back, even though a bag is over 100 yuan now. At jointing time in March, I spread another 15 kilograms of urea per mu. That comes to about 16 kilograms of nitrogen per mu, plus 7 kilograms each of phosphorus and potassium. I irrigate three times from my well: winter water, jointing water, and grain-filling water. Electricity for the pump costs real money, but dry wheat is a disaster. Two sprays are enough—one for weeds early, then one for aphids and rust.

After I cut the wheat in early June, I plant hybrid Zhengdan 958 maize straight into the wheat stubble. No-till. Saves diesel and I do not have time to plow with just me and my wife. Maize needs feeding too. I give it one 50-kilogram bag of compound per mu at sowing, and another 20 kilograms of urea when the plants reach the big trumpet stage. That is about 16 kilograms nitrogen, 6 phosphorus, 6 potassium per mu. Two irrigations in July and August if the rain is short. Two sprays: herbicide right after sowing, then one for corn borer.

Cotton is on 2 mu. I keep it because cash is cash. I use an improved Bt cotton seed. I plow and rotary till that plot in spring to warm the soil. Cotton needs potassium for the bolls, so I give it a full 50-kilogram bag of compound per mu, plus another 10 kilograms of potassium chloride. That works out to about 15 kilograms nitrogen, 7 phosphorus, 8 potassium per mu. I water it three times—seedling, flowering, and boll stage. Three sprays, because bollworm still comes even with Bt cotton, and the aphids love it.

The 2.1 mu of stevia is my gamble. The leaves need to be sweet, so I do not give it too much nitrogen or it grows big leaves with no sweetness. About 10 kilograms nitrogen, 5 phosphorus, 9 potassium per mu. I till it rotary in spring and plant seedlings. It needs water more often, so four irrigations. Two sprays for leaf miners and caterpillars. If I get 180 kilograms of dried leaves per mu, the dealer will buy it.

I always think about last year first. Last year was decent. I will not change much. Better to spend a bit more on fertilizer than to lose yield—a bad harvest means I eat into my savings. I watch the neighbors. If they spray, I spray. If they water, I water. At 66 years old, I do not take risks.
